     TCP also uses ACK clocking, where incoming acknowledgments pace outgoing transmissions, keeping the pipe full      
     while smoothing bursts. Delayed ACKs, cumulative ACKs, and selective acknowledgments (SACK) help the sender        
     distinguish isolated losses from wholesale congestion and retransmit efficiently.                                  
                                                                                                                        
     Newer algorithms address limitations of loss-based AIMD. CUBIC, the Linux default, uses a cubic function of time   
     since the last congestion event, growing aggressively on high-bandwidth long-delay paths and flattening near the   
     previous ceiling. BBR instead models bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip propagation delay, pacing packets to      
     match the estimated capacity and avoiding queue buildup; it does not treat all loss as congestion.                 
                                                                                                                        
     Implementations also tune initial windows, slow-start thresholds, and recovery via algorithms like NewReno,        
     Vegas, and HyStart. The shared goal remains: fill the network pipe efficiently, share capacity fairly with other   
     flows, and back off when congestion signals appear.
